Tomorrow is some sort of monk day.  We will be leaving after breakfast (about 9 am) for a gathering of monks where the governor of Buriram is to be in attendance.

Phra Somboon suggested I have my head shaved, so I said why not.  One of the elder monks shaved my head and then asked if I wanted my eyebrows shaved too.

It never occurred to me that monks shaved their eyebrows, and I never shaved my eyebrows before, so I need to consider this option for a minute.  Why not? So I let him shave my eyebrows as well.

At some level I am considered a monk, but I don't think anyone really knows at what level.  I sit and eat with the monks and not with lay people, but I serve myself after the nun.

I do not attend daily meditations (twice daily at 4 am and 6 pm), and have little idea of the meaning of the prayers and rituals practiced each day at breakfast.

An unusual situation, but everyone is kind, welcoming and non-judgemental.

As for myself, I enjoy the people, the atmosphere, and the group bike rides.  The Thai food is an experience as well.

Today was some sort of regional gathering of monks and nuns.

We the lay-people stayed on the sidelines eating and visiting, and there were vendors present selling the sort of things monks seem to like to buy.

The highlight of their gathering was the reading in Pali language of all the 247 precepts that monks must follow and obey.

The monk who did the reading had to read really fast, because it takes so long to read them all.  I was tempted to record a portion for you to listen as the speed reading was rather remarkable.

Buddha's solution to noise:

A bhikkhu came to the Lord Buddha and complained about a great flock of noisy birds that came to roost at night in the forest surrounding his abode. 

The Buddha suggested that if he wanted them to go away he should go, many times throughout the night, and beg a feather from each bird. 

The birds, thinking, ‘that monk wants a feather, and another, and another…’, left the forest and never returned. 

The Buddha then explained that begging and hinting were unpleasant even to common animals, how much more so to human beings.

Anywhere you go it is all the same.  There are different degrees of positives and negatives to every situation.  When you balance it all out, one situation is as good as another.  There are two exceptions;  the overall friendliness and hospitality of the people toward the stranger (or the foreigner), and money.

Money buys comfort, protection from the elements, whether natural or man-made, refuge, and in some cases, even friendship and trust.

The challenge lies in finding peace, comfort, refuge and hospitality without a great deal of money, and therein lies the value of the overall friendliness and hospitality of the people toward the stranger or the foreigner.

In nations run rampant with fear and distrust for strangers, this can pose a problem for the voyager such as myself.

Last night the dogs at the pagoda were terrible, so I had a bad sleep. Crossing the border was interesting. Lines were long on the Thai departure side, so I just went to the gate without a stamp and told them I did not want to wait in line.  An official approached and I told him the same thing, not expecting in special treatment.  I simply didn't want to wait in line, but was willing to wait until the line grew short however long that may be.  But, surprisingly, for some reason, maybe the looks of me and my bicycle, I was directed to a special window and was treated with the utmost courtesy.  That is what happened on the Thai side ...

There was no line on the Cambodia side, and again there I was treated with great courtesy, but the official said I must remove my Thai flag and replace it with a Cambodian flag, else I may make people angry.  I agreed - seemed reasonable.

Then he came out of his office to look at my bike (he offered me a cigarette which I declined) and suggested I better remove the Thai flag immediately.  No problem - I thought it rather funny that he was looking out for my best interests.

The Thai people are very curious and kind, but also many are shy and reserved.  Nearly everyday in Thailand sometimes several times a đay people will stop the car, motorbike, even tractor ahead of me to take photos.  Sometimes they ask me to stop, and sometimes they just take photos while I ride.

Yesterday, one lady selling corn stopped to give me some corn, while others offer free water, ice, or coffee.  Police are exceptionally nice, wanting to have their photo taken along side of me.  Thailand would be great if it were not for the vicious dogs and loud amplifiers.  Almost paradise - and I feel the prices there are lower than in Cambodia.  One month in Thailand and I did not spend 50 dollars.
